extracted.intended_audience: general newspaper readers interested in labor relations, industrial policy, and national hearings
extracted.subtask_description: A newspaper article reporting negotiations, fact‑finding procedures, company and union positions, and related government/investigative actions in large industrial labor disputes (auto, oil, bus) and concurrent public hearings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-finding board mandate
rubrics_metrics.description: “The board should be * * * directed to make a thorough investigation of all the facts which it deems relevant in the controversy.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board must investigate all relevant facts in a dispute; this is presented as the proper scope of fact‑finding panels hearing labor–management controversies. The article frames this as an explicit instruction/expectation for such boards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to pay as relevant when wages are at issue
rubrics_metrics.description: “When one of the questions at issue is wages, it is essential to enable the board to determine the ability of the employer to pay an increase in wages where such ability is in question.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ability to pay (employer earnings/profits) is a legitimate and essential fact for fact‑finding boards to examine when wage increases are contested; may require access to corporate financial data, forecasts and projections (even speculative future prices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to examine corporate books (use of subpoenas)
rubrics_metrics.description: “To confer the right to examine books is one of the main purposes of granting subpoena power.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Granting subpoena power is justified to allow representatives/officials to inspect companies' books when necessary to determine facts (e.g., ability to pay). The piece discusses subpoena power as central to effective fact‑finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality of employer financial data
rubrics_metrics.description: “The detailed information obtained from the books of an employer should not be made public.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While boards may examine company books, release of detailed financial data publicly is discouraged because it could disadvantage the employer vis‑à‑vis competitors; recommends confidentiality safeguards around financial disclosures to fact‑finding bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on fact‑finding authority regarding price regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Management position: issues within the jurisdiction of OPA (price controls) should not be submitted to the fact‑finding board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Companies may object to fact‑finding boards deciding on matters they consider under other agencies' jurisdiction (e.g., price‑fixing by OPA). The article reports this as a substantive objection to board scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board powers vs. rate‑of‑return setting
rubrics_metrics.description: “This does not mean that the Government, or its fact‑finding board is going to endeavor to fix a rate of return for the employer. It does mean, however, that since wages are paid out of earnings, the question of earnings is relevant.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies that investigating earnings to assess wageability is distinct from regulating company profits; fact‑finding may examine earnings without setting corporate pricing/profit policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary cooperation vs. subpoenaed evidence for tripartite boards
rubrics_metrics.description: Government proposal: boards dependent upon voluntary co‑operation of all parties are envisaged, but proposals also provide power to subpoena documents for major disputes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While tripartite/voluntary cooperation is ideal, effective boards may need statutory subpoena power to compel documents when parties refuse to cooperate; article contrasts voluntary models with proposals that include compulsory powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separating wage issues from other bargaining topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Union demand to have the wage problem separated entirely from other issues in the dispute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Union argued wages should be negotiated independently of other contract items (interplant inequities, vacation pay, pensions, etc.) because packaged concessions can consume a wage offer; presented as a negotiation principle/strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing wage offers against cost of living and inflation risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Union critique: offers (e.g., Ford’s 12.4% or 15¢/hr) are “totally inadequate” and would not meet the present high cost of living or increase purchasing power enough to avoid economic breakdown; also concerns about inflation if price controls are weakened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative standard for judging wage proposals: adequacy relative to current cost of living, purchasing power, and macroeconomic consequences (inflation, breakdown of economy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for settlement in transportation strikes (reinstatement and retroactivity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Greyhound proposal asked companies to reinstate strikers without penalties and make any wage increases finally granted retroactive to November 1, when the strike began.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard settlement terms for transportation strikes include no‑penalty reinstatement and retroactive pay to the strike start date; used as a bargaining demand/condition for returning to work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expedited arbitration procedure for unresolved issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Windsor (Ford Canada) arrangement: matters unresolved after a set time would be submitted to an arbitrator selected from the Canadian Supreme Court for a final ruling within five days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural rubric for rapid resolution: use high‑level arbitration with strict time limits (e.g., five days) to settle outstanding disputes and enable return to work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer security proposals should not absolve company responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Union criticism: management’s “company security” proposal is “unacceptable,” declaring it entirely eliminated all company responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle for acceptable security/contract clauses: they must preserve company accountability (especially regarding supervision and provocation of stoppages); clauses that shift all responsibility to the union are judged unfair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union accountability and penalties for provoking illegal stoppages
rubrics_metrics.description: UAW‑CIO proposal: company and its supervisors be subject to penalties if guilty of provoking illegal work stoppages; the union asserted supervision had provoked stoppages and sought penalties to deter such conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rubric for contract enforcement: include mutual accountability provisions with penalties for management actions that illegally provoke stoppages, rather than unilateral penalization of workers/union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational readiness standard from naval war planning testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Admiral Turner’s standard: under War Plan No. 46, defensive deployment should have sent the Pacific fleet to sea (ready to fight), with extended reconnaissance and submarines dispatched to detect/engage approaching enemy forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criteria for naval readiness: follow pre‑existing war plans that prescribe defensive deployment to sea, reconnaissance coverage, and forward dispositions so forces are in appropriate operating stations to meet the most probable attack vectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional inquiry procedure and time allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Senate‑House committee investigating Pearl Harbor planned extended sessions (six days a week, longer hours), closed‑door witness sequencing, and a target reporting timeline (aim to end hearings by Feb. 15 and report later).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rubric for conducting major Congressional inquiries: schedule intensive hearing blocks, manage witness order strategically (hear some witnesses later), provide extra staff or change counsel as needed, and set realistic reporting deadlines while allowing time to prepare formal findings.
